text:
Good morning, everyone. I found Q3 surprisingly straightforward – it really highlighted where my comfort levels lie with data use. The questions around sensitive data (Q3.5) were harder, precisely *because* they force you to weigh potential benefit against significant ethical concerns.

For me, explainability (Q4) is paramount. As advisors, we need to be able to discuss *why* a student was flagged with them – it builds trust and allows for meaningful support. 

I’m slightly surprised by the strong consensus on accepting up to a 5% accuracy loss for fairness (Q5.1). I initially leaned towards a smaller loss. Perhaps that indicates a willingness to prioritize equity, even at a marginal cost to overall reach – which is positive, but we must monitor unintended consequences closely.

Good morning. I agree with A1 about Q3 being difficult precisely because of the ethical weight – it’s not just a technical question. I also found Q3.4, about Absalon data, tricky. While potentially helpful, tracking online activity *feels* very invasive and crosses a line even if it improves identification slightly.

I think questions around fairness (Q5) are absolutely crucial. As an international student, I’m acutely aware of potential biases, so prioritizing equal recall is important to me. 

My answers on sensitive data were more conservative than some – perhaps because I'm *new* to the Danish system and even more conscious about privacy here. Maybe those who have been here longer feel differently, trusting established safeguards? An opt-out mechanism for data use would definitely ease my concerns.

Good morning, everyone. I found Q3 pretty clear, it was good to walk through those trade-offs explicitly. Q4 felt really important too – especially given my own experience restarting a program. Knowing *why* the system flagged me would be vital; otherwise, it just feels accusatory, not supportive.

I think the biggest difference is probably on admitting & enrolment data (Q3.3). I answered ‘small’ improvement only because past performance isn't always indicative of potential, especially if someone had difficult circumstances. It's easy for that to reinforce existing inequalities. 

The consensus on a 5% accuracy loss for fairness (Q5.1) is reassuring – it suggests people are prioritizing equity which feels right. Perhaps an opt-out would address concerns about data collection in Q3, allowing students more control.

Good morning, everyone. I agree with A1 and S5 – those questions around data sensitivity *are* ethically weighty, not just technical exercises. Q3.4 about Absalon data gave me pause too; while it could be useful, the line between support and surveillance feels thin. As an advisor for 11 years, I’m wary of anything that feels ‘Big Brother’-ish to students.

For me, Q4 – explainability – is fundamental. We *have* to be able to articulate to a student why they were flagged, and what specific supports are relevant. It's about building trust, not just identifying risk. 

I was surprised no one really pushed back against accepting even a moderate improvement for admissions data (Q3.3). I think that’s an area where historical disadvantages could easily be perpetuated, so careful consideration is needed.

Good morning, everyone. I found Q3 surprisingly difficult, especially around deciding what level of improvement justified using more data. It's easy to say "a small improvement is okay" but it’s *my* data being considered, and the line feels blurry.

Q4 about explainability is massively important to me – as someone who’s restarted a programme *and* has ADHD, I need to understand why any system flags me. It's not just trust; it affects my ability to self-advocate. 

I answered 'small' for disability data (Q3.5) because my condition impacts how I study – but it shouldn’t be a negative flag. The group being okay with a 5% accuracy loss for fairness (Q5.1) feels right, though. It shows prioritizing equity over pure efficiency.

Good morning, everyone. I found Q3 quite challenging – especially thinking about Absalon data. As someone who’s started over after dropping out, and learning a new language, I'm already very aware of being *observed*, even unconsciously. Adding more tracking feels…intrusive.

Q4 on explainability resonates deeply; needing to understand *why* is vital. A lack of explanation doesn’t feel like support, it feels like judgment. My answers were conservative regarding sensitive data – I worry about past experiences influencing a model unfairly. 

I think the biggest difference is probably nationality (Q3.5). It's easy to assume struggles are academic when they might be cultural adjustment, and that feels easily missed here. An opt-out would definitely help me feel safer with this system.

Good morning everyone. I found Q3 quite clear, framing the trade-offs well. But Q3.5 – the sensitive data questions – were *really* hard. Coming from outside Denmark, and working part-time while studying, privacy feels especially important to me. While a small improvement in identifying struggling students is tempting, it’s not worth compromising on that for things like nationality or race.

I strongly agree with prioritising explainability (Q4). As an international student, navigating a new system is challenging enough without being flagged by something I don't understand. The 5% accuracy loss for fairness (Q5.1) feels reasonable; equity *is* more important than pure efficiency. Perhaps the biggest difference is my concern about Absalon data - it just feels too much like surveillance.

Good morning, everyone. I found Q3 quite difficult – especially balancing potential help with privacy concerns. As someone managing a long-term mental health condition *and* being an international student, I’m acutely aware of feeling ‘different’. That made the sensitive data questions (Q3.5) particularly challenging; disability data felt… less objectionable if it genuinely linked to support needs. 

I think explainability (Q4) is absolutely critical. Knowing *why* a model flags me is vital for self-advocacy. I was perhaps more conservative than others on admissions data (Q3.3), worried about past circumstances being misinterpreted. The consensus on fairness (Q5) is reassuring, and the opt-out idea feels crucial to building trust.

Good morning, everyone. I found Q3 quite straightforward, honestly – framing the trade-offs helped. But the sensitive data questions (Q3.5) were definitely harder, especially around disability. As someone managing a chronic health condition *while* studying, I see potential benefit in linking that to support, but it needs absolute sensitivity and confidentiality. 

I think explainability (Q4) is vital. Knowing *why* the model flags me as potentially struggling – given my reduced course load last semester – would be crucial for feeling supported, not scrutinised. I was more willing than some to accept a small improvement for Absalon data (Q3.4), but with serious reservations about overreach. The 5% accuracy loss for fairness (Q5.1) feels right; equity needs prioritising.

Good morning, everyone. I found Q3 pretty clear – it was good to really *think* about those trade-offs. The questions around sensitive data (Q3.5) were hardest, though. Being a first-year student with dyslexia, I'm already very conscious of how my learning differences might be perceived. 

I think explainability (Q4) is hugely important – understanding *why* I’m flagged would be vital. I answered ‘small’ for disability data because it genuinely affects how I study, but it shouldn’t define me negatively. The group being okay with a 5% accuracy loss for fairness (Q5.1) feels right; equity matters more. I think nationality might be where we differ – my Danish background maybe makes me less sensitive to those concerns than others.

Good morning, everyone. I found Q3 quite challenging, particularly balancing potential benefit with privacy – having dropped out of a previous program, I’m acutely aware of feeling judged. The sensitive data questions (Q3.5) were difficult; even ‘first-gen’ status feels personal.

Explainability (Q4) is absolutely crucial for me. Knowing *why* the model flagged me would be vital – my restart means past performance isn't a great indicator. I leaned conservative on most data additions, prioritizing privacy. 

I think we differ on Absalon data (Q3.4). While potentially helpful, online activity feels easily misinterpreted and intrusive. The 5% accuracy loss for fairness (Q5.1) is reassuring; equity *has* to be prioritized. An opt-out mechanism would definitely help me feel safer with this system.

Good morning, everyone. I found Q3 quite manageable as an advisor – we're constantly balancing support and privacy already. But Q3.4, Absalon data, gave me pause. While potentially useful, it feels like a step too far towards surveillance; the benefit has to be *very* clear. 

For me, explainability (Q4) is non-negotiable. We need to articulate *why* a student is flagged to build trust and offer meaningful support. My answers around sensitive data leaned cautious - we have a duty of care that extends beyond accuracy. I was surprised by the openness to even moderate improvement for admissions data; past circumstances significantly impact present success, so fairness needs careful consideration there. The opt-out suggestion feels crucial – student agency is paramount.
